title: The basin and towel (John 13:1–15)
hook: at the last supper he kneels and washes their feet
carry: as I have done to you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the perfume, a jar broken over his head. Your line was she has done a beautiful thing. What did you give lavishly? Day sixty. Today, the last supper, and a towel.

Think about feet in that world. Sandals, dusty roads, animals on the streets. When guests arrived for a meal, someone washed their feet. It was the lowest job in the house, the one given to a servant. If there was no servant, nobody volunteered. Now it's the night before Jesus dies. He's at supper with his closest friends, and he knows it's the last. John begins the scene with a sentence like a doorway, in the Douay-Rheims: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end." Unto the end. To the very last. And then, in the middle of the meal, he gets up from the table. Today: the basin and the towel.
screen: `DUSTY FEET, THE LOWEST JOB.` → `THE LAST SUPPER.` → `HE LOVED THEM UNTO THE END.`

segments.voice: John slows down and gives every movement. He rises from supper. He lays aside his outer garments. He takes a towel and ties it around his waist. He pours water into a basin. And he begins to wash the disciples' feet, and to dry them with the towel. The teacher is on his knees, doing the servant's job, going from one friend to the next. And John has already told us that Judas, who will betray him, is at that table. His feet get washed too. Then he comes to Peter, and Peter can't bear it. Lord, are you going to wash my feet? Jesus says: you don't understand now, but you will. And Peter: "Thou shalt never wash my feet." Jesus answers: "If I wash thee not, thou shalt have no part with me." And Peter, all or nothing as always: then not only my feet, Lord, but my hands and my head. When he's finished, Jesus puts his garments back on, sits down, and asks: do you know what I have done to you? You call me Teacher and Lord, and you're right. So if I've washed your feet, you ought to wash one another's. "For I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you do also." Catholics relive this every Holy Thursday, at the Mass of the Lord's Supper. The priest takes off his outer vestment, kneels, and washes the feet of people from the parish. The rite's old Latin name is the Mandatum, from Jesus's new commandment later that night, and that word is where the English name Maundy Thursday comes from.
screen: `HE RISES, TIES ON A TOWEL.` · `JUDAS'S FEET ARE WASHED TOO.` · `PETER: NEVER. THEN, ALL OF ME.` · `HOLY THURSDAY: THE MANDATUM.` · then, large: `AS I HAVE DONE TO YOU, SO YOU DO ALSO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one humble task for someone. Settle and breathe. Think of the jobs nobody wants in your home, your office, your group. Cleaning the bathroom. Taking out the recycling. Staying late to put the chairs away. Changing the diaper. Pick one you could do today for someone else, without being asked, and without mentioning it afterward. Picture yourself doing it slowly, with care, the way John describes the towel and the basin. If you pray, you can offer it for that person. The bell holds the time.
The basin and towel. The night before he died, Jesus knelt and washed his friends' feet, and told them to do the same. Today's word.
Your line: as I have done to you. Today, do the humble task quietly, and let nobody thank you for it. Day sixty.

howItsDone: At the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, the priest washes the feet of members of the congregation, a rite called the Mandatum, after the Gospel of John 13 is read.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 13:1 (second half), 13:8 and 13:15 given from memory; confirm.
The carry 'as I have done to you' matches the Douay-Rheims 13:15 phrase.
Judas's presence at the washing is inferred from 13:2, 13:10–11 and 13:26; the script says 'John has already told us that Judas is at that table'. Confirm.

Holy Thursday Mandatum: optional rite after the homily; since the 2016 decree (Congregation for Divine Worship), those chosen may be any members of the People of God. The script says 'people from the parish'. Confirm.
Maundy from Latin mandatum (John 13:34, 'mandatum novum'): standard etymology; confirm.
